newsitem.title: ITALY: Odds shortening on Italy passing mini-budget soon.
newsitem.headline: Odds shortening on Italy passing mini-budget soon.

text.p: The odds are shortening on Italy's government pushing through a supplementary budget as early as next month to plug a gap in state finances and keep alive a quest to join European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Cabinet undersecretary Enrico Micheli sent a powerful signal that action may be expected sooner rather than later when he said the government should not wait until a quarterly report on state accounts is published in March before making a move.

Micheli said in a television interview on Wednesday night that a supplementary budget was a distinct possibility. "We must look at the accounts. The next days (and) the next weeks" would be important, he said.
"Perhaps we should not even wait for the quarterly accounts to reach a conclusion," he added.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has until now said that no steps would be taken until the quarterly accounts were out.

The government rammed an uncompromising budget through parliament in December tailored to slice 62.5 trillion lire off the public sector deficit budget and ensure Italy makes the grade for EMU membership at the outset in 1999.

But hopes of cutting the public sector deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 1997 -- and thereby meeting one of the key qualifying criteria for joining the single European currency -- were jolted when the Treasury revealed a bigger than expected deficit for 1996.
That leaves the government with an even higher mountain to climb if it is to curb state spending.
Treasury Ministry estimates published last week showed a 1996 public deficit of 138.5 trillion lire ($90 billion), well above a revised government target of 123.0 trillion.
Economists estimate a supplementary budget would have to raise up to 25 trillion lire through spending cuts and tax increases to keep Italy on course for the three percent deficit target.
But it is widely believed that the mini-budget may be more modest in scope, possibly no more than 15 trillion lire.

"If they do it quickly the budget can be smaller in size than if they wait until April or May," said Giovanna Mossetti, an economist at Caboto in Milan. "A 15 trillion lire budget will be hard enough to achieve politically and anything bigger is difficult to imagine," she added.

The centre-left government may be reluctant to raise taxes again on the heels of an unpopular 5.5 trillion lire "Eurotax" which is one of the main planks of its 1997 budget, at a time when the economy is stagnating, economists said.

Newspapers have reported that some three trillion lire could be raised by a "solidarity tax" on Italians who have qualified for pensions by virtue of having worked for more than 35 years but who have not yet reached the statutory retirement age.
Italy's welfare system awards pensions not just based on age but on the number of years worked.
The government wants to phase out early retirements but faces stiff opposition from Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti whose support in parliament is key to its survival.
Prodi last month called on trade union leaders to discuss a revision of the pension system this year but the unions oppose bringing forward the talks, originally scheduled for 1998.

An increase in value added tax is widely seen as another way of quickly raising revenue but the government's hands are tied because of fears of reigniting inflation which is on a firm downward path. ($=1,540 lire)
